Pathology of the Lungs I

PATHO LEC · LE 3 · Trans 4A · Dr. Mesina

Lecture at a Glance

What this lecture covers

  • Introduction: two regions of the respiratory tract, Type I vs Type II pneumocytes, and the clinical manifestations of pulmonary disease (dyspnea, cough, hemoptysis, digital clubbing).
  • Congenital disorders: pulmonary hypoplasia, foregut cysts, pulmonary sequestration.
  • Atelectasis: resorption, compression, contraction, and patchy types.
  • Pulmonary edema: cardiogenic vs non-cardiogenic.
  • Acute lung injury / ARDS: diffuse alveolar damage and hyaline membranes.
  • Obstructive vs restrictive lung disease and spirometry.
  • Obstructive diseases: emphysema, chronic bronchitis, COPD, asthma, bronchiectasis.
  • Chronic diffuse interstitial (restrictive) diseases: IPF, pneumoconioses (CWP, silicosis, asbestosis), complications of therapy, granulomatous disease (sarcoidosis), hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

Main framework

Lung disease
→
Obstructive
  • hard to exhale
  • FEV1/FVC ↓ (<0.7)
vs
Restrictive
  • hard to fully expand
  • FEV1/FVC normal
  • Obstructive group: Emphysema (acinus) · Chronic bronchitis (bronchus) · Asthma (bronchus) · Bronchiectasis (bronchus).
  • Restrictive group: chest wall disorders with normal lungs, and chronic interstitial lung diseases characterized predominantly by inflammation and fibrosis.

Must Know — Red-exclamation points in this lecture
  • Type I pneumocytes are easily injured. Type II pneumocytes are more resistant to injury.
  • Dyspnea: important to distinguish pulmonary vs cardiac origin.
  • Pulmonary hypoplasia: babies delivered prematurely before 28 weeks.
  • Contraction atelectasis is irreversible.
  • ALI/ARDS: 2 initiating events, histology is DAD, hyaline membrane is characteristic.
  • Obstructive: ↓ FEV1, FEV1/FVC < 0.7. Restrictive: proportionate ↓ in TLC and FEV1.
  • Emphysema definition with little or no fibrosis. Centriacinar spares distal alveoli. Panacinar = α1-antitrypsin deficiency, lower zones.
  • COPD is irreversible together with bronchiectasis.
  • Asthma: Curschmann spirals and Charcot-Leyden crystals.
  • Bronchiectasis: 2 major factors in pathogenesis.
  • Restrictive diseases: predominantly inflammation and fibrosis, no sputum production. IPF is prototypic.
  • Pneumoconiosis: 1–5 μm most dangerous. Smaller particle = higher solubility. CWP ≠ cancer or TB.
  • Asbestos bodies are diagnostic. Schaumann and asteroid bodies in sarcoidosis.

A. Respiratory System p. 1–2

Upper AirwayLower Airway
All structures located above the glottic opening
  • Structures below the vocal cords and into the lungs
  • Further subdivided physiologically into:
    • Conducting airways: trachea, bronchi up to terminal bronchioles
      • Where inspired air is conditioned (warming, moistening, filtering) to protect the delicate respiratory tissues
    • Respiratory airways: respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli
      • Where oxygen from inhaled air transfers into the bloodstream while carbon dioxide is exhaled

Respiratory Zone of the Lower Respiratory Tract — Alveolar epithelium

Flat Type I PneumocytesType II Pneumocytes
  • Cover majority of the alveolar surface area (covers 90%)
  • Respiratory unit of the lungs where gas exchange takes place
  • Easily injured Must Know
  • Covers the remaining 10% of alveolar surface
  • Responsible for the synthesis of surfactants
  • Involved in the repair of damaged alveolar epithelium through their ability to proliferate and give rise to or replace injured Type I pneumocytes
  • More resistant to injury Must Know
Figure 3. Healthy lung (L) vs pathologic lung (R) [Lecturer] · p. 2
  • Healthy lung (L): smooth visceral pleural surface. Minimal black specks represent anthracotic or carbon pigments seen in individuals exposed to polluted air.
  • Pathologic lung (R): intense blackening and scarring (unevenness and puckering of the pleural surface). Hyperinflated parenchyma (encircled yellow) representing the pathologic lesions of emphysema.

B. Clinical Manifestations of Pulmonary Diseases p. 2

Dyspnea

  • Shortness of breath or difficulty in breathing that may vary in intensity
  • Important to distinguish this symptom since this can be pulmonary or cardiac in origin Must Know
Dyspnea of pulmonary originDyspnea of cardiac origin
Inability to get a deep breath or increased work of breathingDescribed as suffocation or air hunger associated with heaviness of the chest

If due to a lung pathology, it usually implies poor gas exchange or ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch.

Cough

  • Regarded as a protective reflex to ward off any irritation along the lower airway
  • Becomes pathologic if persistent, chronic, and associated with excessive sputum production

Hemoptysis

  • Coughing or spitting of blood that may originate from the lungs or airways such as the bronchus
  • Usually indicates infection and inflammation that damages the lining of the bronchi

Digital Clubbing

  • Bulbous enlargement of the base of the digits due to increased amounts of connective tissue under the base of the fingernails
  • A non-specific finding, not exclusive to pulmonary disorders
    • Also seen in non-pulmonary chronic conditions like heart diseases associated with chronic hypoxemia

II. Congenital Disorders p. 2–3

  • Rare: 1.4% of congenital disorders of the entire body
  • Considered important because they may lead to considerable morbidity and mortality such as infection, hemorrhage, and respiratory failure
  • Prognosis depends on the size of the lesion and the degree of functional impairment

A. Pulmonary Hypoplasia

Pulmonary Hypoplasia Must Know

  • Definition: Incomplete development of the lung (lobe or distal lung tissue). Usually weighs less than normal with fewer alveoli than expected for gestational age.
  • Who: Usually seen in babies delivered prematurely before 28 weeks of gestation Must Know
  • Cause: Any condition that restricts lung growth, such as congenital diaphragmatic hernia and oligohydramnios. Any factor (direct or indirect) that compromises thoracic space for lung growth.
  • Clinical manifestations: early respiratory distress after birth, cyanosis, tachypnea, hypoxia, hypercapnia, acidosis
Figure 4. Gross specimen of pulmonary hypoplasia. Encircled: underdeveloped lung with reduced lung weight to body weight ratio [Lecturer] · p. 2

B. Foregut Cysts

  • Arise from an abnormal budding or detachment of the primitive foregut during fetal development
    • Mechanism of development remains unknown
  • Commonly located in the hilum or middle mediastinum
  • Many are asymptomatic, but incidental findings may be observed on chest radiography
  • Infection, hemorrhage, and malignancy (rare) can occur
  • May come to attention when they cause respiratory symptoms: cough, dyspnea, or hemoptysis (if symptomatic: dyspnea, atelectasis, or hyperinflation with obstructive symptoms)
  • Excellent prognosis when there is complete excision of the lesion

Types of Foregut Cysts (3 types)

TypeKey features
Bronchogenic cyst
  • Most common
  • Gross: unilocular, delicate thin-walled cyst
  • Microscopic: lining is smooth, composed of pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium
  • Rarely connected to the tracheobronchial tree
  • Cyst wall may contain seromucinous glands, hyaline cartilage, or smooth muscle
Esophageal cystLined by squamous epithelium
Enteric cystThird type of foregut cyst

C. Pulmonary Sequestration

  • Lobes or segments of lung tissue without a normal connection to the airway system
  • Arterial blood supply is from the aorta and its branches, and not from the pulmonary arteries

Classification based on location (2 types)

Extralobar sequestrationIntralobar sequestration
LocationExternal to the lungWithin the lung
Age / presentationSeen in infants, presenting as mass lesionsSeen in older children, presenting with recurrent localized infection or bronchiectasis
Figure 6 (L). Intralobar vs extralobar sequestration [Lecturer's PPT] · p. 3
Figure 6 (R). Gross pulmonary sequestration · p. 3
Clinical Cue
  • Infant with a mass lesion outside the lung → extralobar.
  • Older child with recurrent localized infection or bronchiectasis → intralobar.

III. Atelectasis p. 4

  • Definition: Loss of lung volume due to incomplete expansion of the lungs
  • May be due to:
  • Insufficient surfactant (neonatal atelectasis)
  • Collapse of a previously inflated lung (acquired atelectasis, as seen in adults)
  • Clinical implications:
  • Reduction in oxygenation
  • Predisposition to respiratory infection
Figure 7. Gross atelectatic lung — note the dark red violaceous color of the collapsed lower lobe or segment [Lecturer's PPT] · p. 4

A. Types of Acquired Atelectasis Based on Mechanism

Resorption / Obstruction Atelectasis

  • Occurs from the complete obstruction of the airway over time
    • Air retained distal to the occlusion is resorbed from non-ventilated alveoli → affected regions become totally gasless and then collapse
  • The mediastinum shifts toward the atelectatic lung
  • Reversible
  • Causes: foreign body, intrabronchial tumors, mucus plugging (excessive secretions, exudates within small bronchi)
    • Obstruction can occur at any level of the larger or smaller bronchus
  • Can be seen in: asthma (mucus plugs obstructing the airway), chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis, post-operative states (especially under general anesthesia, with retention of secretions)
    • This is why postoperative patients are encouraged to take deep breathing exercises to re-expand the patchy atelectatic areas

Compression Atelectasis

  • Occurs when a significant amount of fluid (blood, effusions, exudate), solid material (tumor), or air (pneumothorax) accumulates in the pleural cavity and displaces or compresses the lung tissue
    • Pressure impinges on and threatens the function of the lung and mediastinum, especially the major vessels
  • Reversible
  • The mediastinum shifts away from the atelectatic lung
  • Examples: pleural effusion, pneumothorax

Contraction Atelectasis

  • Occurs when there is focal or generalized pulmonary fibrosis, preventing full expansion of the lung parenchyma
  • Irreversible Must Know
    • Since scarring or fibrosis causes permanent non-expansion of the lung tissue
  • The mediastinum does not shift
  • Example: severe parenchymal scarring

Patchy Atelectasis

  • Usually attributed to loss of surfactant, as seen in acute respiratory distress syndrome
  • Reversible
Figure 8. Various forms of acquired atelectasis. Dashed lines indicate normal lung volume [Lecturer's PPT] · p. 4
Notice the direction of the mediastinal shift (red arrows): toward the collapse in resorption, away in compression, and none in contraction.
TypeMechanismMediastinumReversible?Examples
Resorption / ObstructionComplete airway obstruction → distal air resorbedShifts towardYesForeign body, tumors, mucus plugs (asthma, chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis, post-op)
CompressionFluid, solid, or air in the pleural cavity compresses the lungShifts awayYesPleural effusion, pneumothorax

IV. Pulmonary Edema p. 4–5

Definition Must Know

Escape or leakage of excessive interstitial fluid from the intravascular compartment into the alveolar space and interstitium, resulting from hemodynamic disturbances or microvascular injury.

Lecturer's must-know wording: extravasation of fluid from the pulmonary vasculature into the interstitium and alveoli of the lungs.

Hemodynamic disturbance
→
Cardiogenic edema
↑ vascular permeability due to microvascular injury
→
Non-cardiogenic edema

Classification (based on underlying causes)

Cardiogenic Pulmonary Edema (CPE)

  • Mechanism: Imbalance of Starling forces
  • Pressure drives the imbalance that produces edema
  • Examples: Left-sided heart failure (most common), LV hypertrophy & cardiomyopathy, dysrhythmia, myocardial infarction, LV outflow obstruction

Pathology of CPE (Figure 9)

Left sided heart failure
↓
Decreased pumping ability to the systemic circulation
↓
Congestion and accumulation of blood in pulmonary area
↓
Fluid leaks out of intravascular space to the interstitium
↓
Accumulation of fluid
↓
Pulmonary edema

Non-Cardiogenic Pulmonary Edema

  • Mechanism: damage to alveolar-capillary barrier / lymphatic obstruction / damage of endothelial barrier causing permeability of alveolar basement membrane
  • Mostly involves inflammatory cells like neutrophils and macrophages that promote inflammatory cytokines → further injury to alveolar and epithelial capillaries → increased permeability of barrier
  • Examples: bacterial pneumonia (edema fluid and infiltrates), smoke inhalation, radiation, lung trauma, systemic inflammatory response syndrome (sepsis, burns, pancreatitis, extensive trauma), blood transfusion-related
Figure 10. Comparison of cardiogenic (L) to noncardiogenic (R) pulmonary edema · p. 5
Left: increased hydrostatic pressure pushes protein-poor fluid out. Right: injured endothelium and epithelium leak protein-rich fluid with inflammatory cells.

↑ hydrostatic pressure (↑ pulmonary venous pressure)Left-sided heart failure (common), volume overload, pulmonary vein obstruction
↓ oncotic pressure (less common)Hypoalbuminemia, nephrotic syndrome, liver disease, protein-losing enteropathies
Lymphatic obstructionRare, secondary to ↑ hydrostatic pressure
Edema Due to Alveolar Wall Injury (Microvascular or Epithelial Injury)
Direct injury
  • Infections: bacterial pneumonia
  • Inhaled gases: high-concentration oxygen, smoke
  • Liquid aspiration: gastric contents, near-drowning
  • Radiation
Indirect injury
  • Septicemia
  • Blood transfusion-related
  • Burns

  • Shock, trauma
Edema of Undetermined Origin
High altitude · Neurogenic (central nervous system trauma)

A. Morphology of Pulmonary Edema

Figure 11. Morphology of pulmonary edema [Lecturer's PPT] · p. 5
  • (L) Gross: lungs are wet and heavier than normal. Frothy fluid (yellow arrow) oozes from the cut surface.
  • (R) Histology: alveolar walls/septae show stasis or congestion of RBC within dilated alveolar capillaries. Alveolar spaces are filled with pinkish homogenous material, which is the edema fluid.

V. Acute Lung Injury (ALI) p. 5–7

  • Also known as noncardiogenic pulmonary edema
  • Abrupt onset of significant hypoxemia and diffuse bilateral pulmonary infiltrates in the absence of cardiac failure
  • A disorder of acute lung inflammation that causes disruption or injury of the lung endothelial and epithelial cells
  • Complication of several underlying conditions: either a direct injury to the lungs or a systemic disorder
  • Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS): clinical manifestation of the severe form of ALI
Must Know — 2 important initiating events of ALI / ARDS
  • 1. Damage to pulmonary endothelium and Type I alveolar epithelial cells (Type I pneumocytes)
  • 2. Presence of inflammation and pulmonary damage

A. Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)

  • Clinical manifestation of the severe form of ALI
    • Progressive respiratory insufficiency due to diffuse alveolar damage
  • Almost always associated with inflammation
  • Histological manifestation of this disease is Diffuse Alveolar Damage (DAD) Must Know
  • Interchangeable with ALI, but ARDS is the preferred term for clinical diagnosis
ARDSALI
  • Clinical term
  • Clinical manifestation of extreme or severe ALI
  • Pathologic term
  • Abrupt onset of hypoxemia and bilateral pulmonary edema in the absence of cardiac failure
  • Histologic picture: Diffuse Alveolar Damage (DAD)
Table 3. Conditions associated with development of ARDS (* = common conditions giving rise to ALI)
CategoryConditions
Infection
  • Sepsis*
  • Diffuse pulmonary infections* (viral, Mycoplasma, Pneumocystis pneumonia, miliary tuberculosis)
  • Gastric aspiration*
Physical injury
  • Mechanical trauma, including head injuries*
  • Pulmonary contusions, near-drowning, fractures with fat embolism, burns, ionizing radiation
Inhaled irritantsOxygen toxicity, smoke, irritant gases and chemicals
Chemical injuryHeroin or methadone overdose, acetylsalicylic acid, barbiturate overdose, paraquat
Hematologic conditionsMultiple transfusions, disseminated intravascular coagulation
OthersPancreatitis · Uremia · Cardio-pulmonary bypass · Hypersensitivity reactions (organic solvents, drugs)

Pathogenesis of ARDS

Acute lung injury is a result of:

  • Loss of alveolar capillary membrane integrity
  • Excessive transepithelial neutrophil migration
  • Release of proinflammatory cytotoxic mediators

4 Phases

1. Endothelial activation
  • Pneumocyte injury detected by resident alveolar macrophages → activated macrophages release IL-1 and TNF → activate and damage the endothelium
↓
2. Adhesion and extravasation of neutrophils
  • Neutrophils adhere to activated endothelium and migrate into interstitium and alveolar spaces
  • They degranulate and release proteases, reactive oxygen species (ROS), and cytokines → damage Type I pneumocytes
  • Results in a vicious cycle of ongoing endothelial and epithelial injury
↓
3. Accumulation of intra-alveolar fluid and formation of hyaline membrane
  • Endothelial injury → ↑ vascular permeability → leakage of fluid into epithelium and alveolar spaces
  • Type I pneumocytes undergo necrosis
  • Type II pneumocytes are injured → impaired surfactant production
  • Protein-rich fluid and cellular debris organize into pink, waxy hyaline membranes lining the alveoli
  • Hyaline membranes impair gas exchange, affecting both ventilation and perfusion
↓
4. Resolution of injury
  • Resolution is slow and difficult, influenced by severity and cause
  • Inflammation must subside before healing can occur
  • Resident macrophages remove debris and release fibrogenic cytokines TGF-β and PDGF → fibroblast proliferation → fibrosis of alveolar walls
  • Type II pneumocytes proliferate to replace lost Type I pneumocytes, restoring the alveolar lining
  • Endothelial repair as uninjured capillary endothelial cells proliferate
Figure 12. Pathogenesis of ARDS and ALI — normal alveolus (L) vs acute lung injury (R) [Lecturer's PPT] · p. 6
Acute phase (right side): sloughing of bronchial and alveolar epithelial cells with a protein-rich hyaline membrane on the denuded basement membrane. Neutrophils adhere to injured capillary endothelium and marginate through the interstitium toward the airspace filled with protein-rich edema fluid. Endothelial activation makes capillaries leaky → hyaline membrane, characteristic of ALI/ARDS Must Know. Alveolar macrophages secrete IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, TNF-α → chemotaxis and activation of neutrophils. IL-1 also stimulates extracellular matrix by fibroblasts. Neutrophils release oxidants, proteases, leukotrienes, and platelet activating factor. 30 minutes after an acute insult: ↑ IL-8 synthesis.

Fate of the acute phase of ALI

ResolvedWith no sequelae
ProgressTo a protracted phase of persistent respiratory failure: persistent hypoxemia and decreased lung compliance. Histologically fibrosis with acute and chronic inflammation and partial resolution of edema

Morphology of ALI

Figure 13. (L) Gross and (R) histology of ALI · p. 7
Figure 14. Formation of hyaline membrane in the early phase · p. 7
GrossHistology
Diffuse involvement with firm, non-crepitant, and rubbery consistency
  • Scattered neutrophils and macrophages
  • Necrosis of alveolar epithelial cells
  • Formation of hyaline membranes
  • Interstitial inflammation and fibrosis
Must Know — Microscopic features of DAD (acute phase)
  • Presence of hyaline membranes lining the alveolar walls: composed of dead or injured epithelial cell debris that meshes with fibrin and other plasma proteins in the fluid.
  • Edema fluid mixed with remnants of necrotic epithelial cells.
  • Collapsed alveoli and neutrophilic infiltration.
Lecturer's Note — Sepsis pathway (Must Knows box) Patient with sepsis → uncontrolled infiltration of neutrophils and macrophages → inflammatory cytokines (TNFα and IL) → neutrophilic infiltration in lung tissue → neutrophils release enzymes and reactive oxygen species → direct injury to alveolar epithelial cells and alveolar capillary membrane → increased vascular and alveolar permeability (early phases).

Clinical Presentation / Course of ALI/ARDS

  • Course is variable: depends on the nature of the causal process (and reversibility), age, and early accurate therapeutic intervention
  • Factors which influence mortality: patient's age and previously existing organ dysfunction
  • If the patient survives:
    • Develop fibrosis with signs and symptoms typical of obstructive airway diseases
    • Complete recovery, normal respiratory function within 6–12 months after the acute episode

VI. Obstructive vs Restrictive Lung Diseases p. 7–8

Both types may cause shortness of breath

Obstructive lung diseaseRestrictive lung disease
Conditions that make it hard for an individual to exhale all the air in the lungsDifficulty for an individual in fully expanding their lungs with air

Table 4. Obstructive vs Restrictive

FeatureOBSTRUCTIVERESTRICTIVE
ProblemObstruction or resistance to air movement in and out of the lungsRestriction or limitation to full expansion of the lungs
TLC / FVCTLC and FVC are normal or slightly increasedFVC is reduced
FEV1/FVC ratioDecreasedIncreased or near normal
HallmarkMarked by decreased expiratory flow (FEV1) Must KnowProportionate ↓ in TLC and FEV1
Causes / conditionsAsthma, emphysema, chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis, bronchiolitis
  • Chest wall disorders (with normal lungs): severe obesity, disease of the pleura, kyphoscoliosis, neuromuscular disorders such as GBS
  • Chronic interstitial lung diseases: pneumoconiosis, interstitial fibrosis of unknown etiology, infiltrative conditions (sarcoidosis)

Pulmonary Function Test (Spirometry)

Pulmonary function test (AKA spirometry) is a useful tool in the diagnosis and management of these two diseases.

ObstructiveRestrictive
  • ↓ maximal airflow rates during forced expiration (↓ FEV at 1 second, FEV1) over the forced ventilatory capacity (FVC)
  • FEV1/FVC ratio = ↓ (< 0.7 or 70%) → airway obstruction Must Know
  • Proportionate ↓ in both total lung capacity and FEV1 Must Know
  • FEV1/FVC ratio remains normal (0.75–0.80 or 75–80%)
Normal FEV1/FVC ratio: 0.75 – 0.80 (75–80%) · Obstruction: < 0.7 (70%)

Restrictive lung diseases are classified into two

Restrictive lung diseases
  • Chest wall disorders in the presence of normal lungs
    • Severe obesity, disease of the pleura, kyphoscoliosis, neuromuscular disorders (e.g., GBS) that affect the respiratory muscles
  • Disorders that involve the lung parenchyma
    • Chronic interstitial and infiltrative disease: pneumoconiosis, interstitial fibrosis of unknown etiology, infiltrative conditions such as sarcoidosis

Figure 22 (Lecturer's Must Knows) — Obstructive vs Restrictive

OBSTRUCTIVERESTRICTIVE
  • Characterized by reduction in airflow
  • Shortness of breath → in exhaling air (air remains inside the lung after full expiration)
  • 1. Emphysema
  • 2. Chronic bronchitis → COPD
  • 3. Bronchial asthma
  • 4. Bronchiectasis
  • Spirometry: Decreased in FEV1 and FEV1/FVC ratio
  • Reduction in lung volume
  • Difficulty of taking air inside the lung (due to stiffness inside the lung or within chest wall cavity)
  • 1. Interstitial lung disease
  • 2. Scoliosis
  • 3. Marked obesity
  • 4. Neuromuscular disorders
  • Spirometry: Normal FEV1/FVC ratio
Exam Trap
  • In restrictive disease the FEV1 is also reduced, but proportionately with TLC, so the ratio stays normal.
  • In obstructive disease the ratio falls because FEV1 drops while FVC is normal or slightly increased.

VII. Obstructive Lung Diseases p. 8

  • Group of respiratory lung conditions characterized by airway obstruction
    • Primarily affects the smaller bronchi or larger bronchioles
    • Difficult for air to flow out of the lung → difficulty in exhaling air
  • Common obstructive diseases:
    • Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD): 2 major clinicopathologic manifestations — Emphysema and Chronic Bronchitis. Commonly associated with each other as they share the same underlying cause: chronic cigarette smoking
    • Asthma
    • Bronchiectasis

Clinical TermLocationPathologic ChangesEtiology

A. Emphysema p. 8–11

Definition Must Know

  • Permanent, abnormal, enlargement of the airspaces distal to the terminal bronchioles (all portions of the respiratory unit)
    • Accompanied with destruction of their walls / alveolar septae with little or no fibrosis Must Know
  • Lecturer: Irreversible enlargement of the airspaces distal to the terminal bronchiole, accompanied by destruction of their walls
  • Associated with loss of elastic recoil and support of small airways → tendency to collapse with obstruction

Classification of Emphysema

Figure 15. Classification of emphysema — centrilobular, panlobular, paraseptal, irregular [Lecturer's PPT] · p. 8
Notice which part of the acinus is dilated: the center (centrilobular), the whole acinus (panlobular), the distal/peripheral part (paraseptal), or irregular involvement with scarring.

Centriacinar / Centrilobular Emphysema

  • Most common form of emphysema
    • Consequence of cigarette smoking
    • Form seen in COPD
  • Affects the central or proximal parts of the acini formed by the bronchioles → distal alveoli are unaffected Must Know
  • Predominant among heavy cigarette smokers
  • Lesions more common and pronounced in upper lobes, specifically the apical segments
  • Both emphysematous and normal airspaces exist within the same acinus

Panacinar / Panlobular Emphysema

  • Associated with α1-antitrypsin deficiency Must Know
  • Affects the acini from the level of the respiratory bronchiole to the terminal alveoli → uniformly enlarged
  • In contrast to centriacinar: occurs more commonly in the lower zones and anterior margins of the lung, usually severe at the bases Must Know
  • Gross: all portions of acini are distended with thin & stretched alveolar walls
  • Histologically: spurs of broken septa due to rupture of alveolar walls

Distal / Paraseptal Emphysema

  • Affects the distal acini → spares the proximal portion
  • Predominant in young adults with spontaneous pneumothorax
  • More striking adjacent to the pleura, along the lobular connective tissue septa and at the margins of the lobules
  • Associated in areas of fibrosis and scarring

Irregular Emphysema

  • Named as such due to acinus being irregularly involved and invariably associated with scarring
  • Clinically insignificant

Table 6. Classifications of Emphysema

FormCauseLocationOther Features
Centriacinar / CentrilobularSmokingAirspace enlargement and destruction (central acinus, upper lobes)Tobacco smoke
Panacinar / PanlobularLack of α1-antitrypsinLower zones and anterior marginsGenetic deficiency of α1-antitrypsin
Distal (Paraseptal)Areas of scarring, fibrosis and atelectasisNear the pleura and along the lobular septa/marginSpontaneous pneumothorax in young adults
IrregularAssociated with scarring—Insignificant
Must Know — Two clinically significant forms
  • Centriacinar and Panacinar lead to significant deterioration of respiratory function if no medical intervention is provided.
  • The 2 conditions are related to chronic smoking and α1-antitrypsin, respectively.
  • Pathogenesis results from consequences of 2 critical imbalances.
Lecture memory aid — "Cigarettes Is Primary Problem"
  • Types: Centriacinar, Irregular, Panacinar, Paraseptal.
  • Most important feature for each: Cigarette · Inflammation healed to scar · Protease inhibitor deficiency (α1-antitrypsin) · Pneumothorax.

Pathogenesis of Emphysema

Causes and factors

  • Causes: Smoking · Noxious particles (air pollutants) · Genetic predisposition (congenital α1-antitrypsin deficiency)
  • Factors associated with development:
  • Inflammatory cells, release of inflammatory mediators: neutrophils, activated macrophages, CD8+ lymphocytes accumulate and release proteases and inflammatory mediators → degradation of extracellular matrix of the alveoli
  • Oxidative stress from cigarette smoking: ROS from smoke stimulates additional ROS from inflammatory cells → further tissue damage and inflammation
  • Protease-antiprotease imbalance: inflammation and oxidative damage compromise alveolar wall integrity → emphysema

Figure 16 flow (recreated)

Smoking
Air pollutants
Genetic predisposition (congenital α1-antitrypsin deficiency)
Oxidative stress, increased apoptosis and senescence
Inflammatory cells, release of inflammatory mediators (LTB4, IL-8, TNF)
Protease-antiprotease imbalance
↓
Alveolar wall destruction (Emphysema)

The 2 critical imbalances Must Know

Protease-antiprotease imbalanceOxidant-antioxidant imbalance
  • Genetic deficiency of antiprotease α1-antitrypsin → Panacinar type
  • An individual with this deficiency who smokes induces the influx of neutrophils → release of proteases in the form of elastase
  • In the absence of α1-antitrypsin → excessive digestion of elastic tissue → emphysema
  • α1-antitrypsin is protective and is inhibited by smoking
  • More related to centriacinar emphysema with heavy smoking
  • Cigarette smoking increases elastase availability and decreases anti-elastase activity
  • Tobacco smoke contains abundant ROS (free radicals) which deplete antioxidant mechanisms → functional deficiency of α1-antitrypsin → tissue damage
  • Tissue breakdown enhanced by inactivation of protective antiproteases by ROS

Lecturer's example: patient smokes → inflammation in bronchial tree → ↑ neutrophils and macrophages in alveoli → release neutrophil elastase and enhanced macrophage elastase activity → tissue damage. Chronic smoker → tobacco ROS inactivate anti-proteases → functional deficiency → further damage.

Figure 17. Pathogenesis of emphysema [Lecturer's PPT] · p. 9
Tobacco → neutrophil elastase and macrophage elastase/metalloproteinases, plus ROS → inactivation of antiproteases ("functional" α1-AT deficiency). Congenital α1-AT deficiency feeds the same end point: emphysema.

Morphology of Emphysema

GrossCentriacinarPanacinar
Both forms: enlargement of air spaces
  • Emphysematous air spaces surrounded by relatively normal air spaces
  • Related to cigarette smoking
  • Lungs are a deeper pink and less voluminous than in panacinar
  • Almost entire alveoli are enlarged
  • Related to α1-antitrypsin deficiency
  • Pale, voluminous lungs
Figure 18. Clinically significant types: centriacinar (L) vs panacinar (R) · p. 9
Figure 19. Centriacinar (L): central areas with marked damage surrounded by spared alveoli. Panacinar (R): entire lobule involved · p. 9

Bullous Emphysema

  • Morphologic variant of emphysema
  • Damaged alveoli distend to form exceptionally large air spaces greater than 1 cm
  • Located subpleurally
  • Can occur in any form of emphysema and has potential to rupture → pneumothorax
Figure 20. Bullous emphysema — large subpleural bullae · p. 10

Histologically

  • Marked dilatation of the alveolar spaces with destruction of alveolar septa
  • Enlargement of air spaces with destruction of septa but without fibrosis. Note the presence of black anthracotic pigment.
Figure 21. Pulmonary emphysema histology — enlarged air spaces, destroyed septa, black anthracotic pigment (arrow) · p. 10

Clinical Features of Emphysema

  • Signs and symptoms only start to appear when 1/3 or more of the functioning pulmonary tissue is damaged
  • Dyspnea: usual primary clinical manifestation, progressive
    • Initially only on exertion, then steadily worsens and manifests even at rest
    • May be associated with chronic cough producing mucus, chest tightness, fatigue, and weight loss as disease advances
  • Clinical course: periodic exacerbation triggered by infection, air pollution, inflammation → worsening of emphysema
  • Progression / complications:
    • Pulmonary hypertension → Cor pulmonale (cor pulmonale most commonly arises from complications of high blood pressure in the pulmonary arteries)
    • Congestive heart failure (right-sided): with cor pulmonale related to secondary pulmonary hypertension — associated with poor prognosis
  • Signs: thorax has an elliptical shape with anteroposterior-to-transverse 1:1
    • Trapped air pushes soft tissue of the ribcage so AP diameter increases to 1:1
    • Normal diameter documented as 1:2 or 0.70
  • CXR: Normal (without emphysema) = fine vascular markings. With emphysema = hyperlucent lungs (air obliterated the vasculature)
Figure 23. AP diameter of patient with emphysema (barrel chest) · p. 10
Figure 24. Hyperlucent lungs on CXR · p. 11
Must Know — Emphysema recap (2027 box)
  • Irreversible abnormal enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchioles with destruction of walls/alveolar septae with little or without fibrosis.
  • Macroscopic: centriacinar — less remarkable, deeper pink, less voluminous. Panacinar — pale, voluminous lungs.
  • Microscopic: destruction of alveolar walls without fibrosis → enlarged airspaces.
  • Types: Centriacinar — upper lobes, smokers. Irregular — clinically insignificant. Panacinar — lower zones, lack of α1-antitrypsin. Paraseptal/Distal — areas of scarring, spontaneous pneumothorax.
  • Mechanism: release of elastase from neutrophils.

B. Chronic Bronchitis p. 11–12

Clinical Definition Must Know

Persistent cough with sputum production for at least 3 months per year in at least 2 consecutive years in the absence of any other identifiable cause.

  • Etiology: exposure to noxious or irritating substances
  • Most common cause: tobacco smoking
  • Minor causes: inhaled pollutants (dust from grain, fumes, and silica)

Pathogenesis of Chronic Bronchitis

Initiating factor: chronic exposure to inhaled irritant substance
  • (tobacco smoke, dust from grain, cotton, dust)
↓
Inflammation of the airways
↓
Hypertrophy of submucosal glands in the bronchial walls
↓
Mucus hypersecretion
↓
Episodes of acute bronchitis
Productive cough

Continuous inflammation and excess mucus production → narrow airway lumen and ↓ airflow. Bronchioles are clogged with mucus, which poses as a physical barrier to ventilation.

Figure 27 — Histologic changes of chronic bronchitis (recreated)

Chronic irritation of bronchial mucosa by inhaled irritant substances like TOBACCO SMOKE, dust, grain dust, silica
↓
Excess of mucus producing GOBLET CELLS in the lining epithelium
↓
Hyperplasia and hypertrophy of the SUBMUCOSAL GLANDS
↓
INFLAMMATION and excess mucus production in the small airways (bronchiolitis)
↓
Chronic inflammation of small & large airways leading to FIBROSIS

Morphology of Chronic Bronchitis

GrossHistologically
  • Hyperemia, swelling, and edema of the mucosal lining of the bronchus
  • Frequently accompanied by excessive mucous secretions
  • Striking change: increase in size of the mucous glands
  • Mild chronic inflammation of the airways (predominantly leukocytes)
  • Fibrous replacement of the muscular wall of small bronchioles (chronic obstructive bronchitis)
Figure 26. Histology of chronic bronchitis — normal (L) vs mucous gland hyperplasia (R) [Lecturer's PPT] · p. 11

Reid Index Must Know

  • Ratio of thickness of the mucous gland layer (arrow C–D) to the thickness of the wall between the basement layer of the epithelium and the cartilage (arrow A–B)
  • Normal value: 0.4
  • Increased in chronic bronchitis due to thickened mucous gland layer
    • Increase is proportional to the severity and duration of bronchitis
Reid index = mucous gland layer thickness ÷ bronchial wall thickness (epithelium basal layer → cartilage) · Normal 0.4
Figure 28. Reid index — normal vs chronic bronchitis · p. 12

Clinical Features of Chronic Bronchitis

  • Cardinal symptom: persistent productive cough
  • Can predispose to recurrent pulmonary infection as a secondary complication
  • Long standing severe chronic bronchitis may lead to cor pulmonale and heart failure
  • Bronchial epithelium may also exhibit atypical metaplasia and dysplasia
    • Due to the irritating and mutagenic effects of substances like tobacco smoke → predisposing to cancerous transformation

C. Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) p. 12

  • Progressive lung disease as a result of chronic airflow obstruction and inflation
  • Pathologically involves chronic bronchitis and emphysema since both share a similar background of exposure to tobacco smoke
  • Gives rise to irreversible airflow obstruction, which distinguishes it from asthma (largely reversible)
  • Clinical picture varies according to severity and the relative contributions of emphysematous and bronchitic changes
    • Pink puffers — predominantly emphysema: barrel-chested, early symptoms of dyspnea
    • Blue bloaters — predominantly chronic bronchitis: first cardinal manifestation is persistent productive cough
Must Know — COPD
  • Emphysema + chronic bronchitis clinically grouped together. One predominates from one another.
  • Irreversible airflow obstruction, together with bronchiectasis.

Table 7. Chronic Bronchitis vs Emphysema

FeaturePredominant BronchitisPredominant Emphysema
Age (years)40–4550–75
DyspneaMild, appears lateSevere, appears early
CoughEarly, copious sputumLate, scanty sputum
InfectionsCommonOccasional
Respiratory insufficiencyRepeatedTerminal
Cor pulmonaleCommonRare, terminal
Airway resistanceIncreasedNormal or slightly increased
Elastic recoilNormalLow
Chest radiographProminent vessels, large heartHyperinflation, small heart
Appearance"Blue bloater""Pink puffer"

Both affected → COPD (common)

Clinical Course of COPD

  • Long standing COPD: development of cor pulmonale and eventually congestive heart failure related to secondary pulmonary hypertension
  • Death due to COPD:
    • Right sided heart failure
    • Collapse of lung secondary to pneumothorax (emphysema)
    • Intercurrent bacterial infection (bronchitis)
    • Acute respiratory failure due to complicated pulmonary infections superimposed on COPD

D. Asthma p. 13–14

Definition and Hallmarks Must Know

  • Characterized by chronic airway inflammation and variable expiratory airflow obstruction
    • Cardinal manifestation: recurrent episodes of wheezing, breathlessness, chest tightness, and cough, particularly at night and/or early morning
  • Differs from other obstructive lung diseases in that it is largely reversible, either spontaneously or with treatment
  • Hallmarks:
    • Intermittent and reversible airway obstruction
    • Chronic bronchial inflammation with eosinophils
    • Bronchial smooth muscle cell hypertrophy and hyper-reactivity → increased mucus production
  • Classified based on the stimuli that trigger bronchoconstriction: Atopic (Extrinsic) or Non-atopic (Intrinsic)

Table 8. Atopic vs Non-atopic Asthma

FeatureAtopic / "Extrinsic"Non-atopic / "Intrinsic"
MechanismType I hypersensitivityNon-immune
StimulantsEnvironmental allergens: dander, dust, pollen, foodAspirin ingestion, viral infections, cold, chemicals and fumes, stress, exercise
Age of presentationChildhoodAdulthood
Family historyPositiveNegative
History of other allergic diseasesPositiveNegative
Skin testPositiveNegative
Serum IgE levelHighNormal

Pathogenesis of Atopic Asthma

Inhaled allergen elicits a T-helper 2 response
↓
Secretion of cytokines that promote inflammation and stimulate B cells to produce IgE
  • Cytokines also recruit eosinophils
↓
IgE binds to receptors on mast cells
↓ repeated exposure / re-exposure
Antigen-induced cross-linking of IgE bound to Fc receptors on mast cells → release of granule contents, cytokines, and other mediators
↓
Early phase reaction (immediate hypersensitivity)
  • Preformed mediators act directly and via neuronal reflexes to induce:
  • Bronchospasm
  • Increased vascular permeability & mucus production
  • Recruitment of leukocytes
Late phase reactionLeukocytes are recruited to the site and WBCs release additional mediators that initiate the late phase reaction
Figure 29. Pathogenesis of atopic asthma — normal airway, triggering, airway in asthma, immediate and late phase [2027] · p. 13

Non-atopic (Intrinsic) Asthma

  • Less common than atopic asthma
  • Inflammation and restriction of the airway not caused by exposure to an allergen
  • Triggered by: respiratory viral tract infections (rhino-, influenza), air pollutants, aspirin. Others: exercise, cold
  • No common family history of asthma · Serum IgE levels are normal · No allergies

Pathogenesis of non-atopic asthma

  • Mechanism of bronchial inflammation and hyperresponsiveness is less clear
  • Triggered by viral infection of the respiratory tract (the most common stimulus) and inhaled air pollutants (sulfur dioxide, ozone, nitrogen dioxide)
  • Viral-induced inflammation of the respiratory mucosa lowers the threshold of the epithelial vagal receptors to irritants → hypersensitivity of the airways

Morphology of Asthma

  • Gross: in severe asthma, the most striking feature is the occlusion of the bronchi & bronchioles by thick, tenacious mucus plugs, which often contain shed epithelium
  • Classic histologic features:
  • Mucus hypersecretion with clogging
  • Narrowing of the lumen
  • Smooth muscle hypertrophy
  • Infiltration of lymphocytes or eosinophils of the bronchial wall
  • Thickening of basement membrane
  • Edema and inflammatory infiltrates in bronchial wall
  • Submucosal gland increases
  • Mucus containing Curschmann spirals, eosinophils, Charcot-Leyden crystals
Figure 30. Morphology of asthma — mucus plug and thickened bronchial wall [Lecturer's PPT] · p. 14

Curschmann spirals and Charcot-Leyden crystals Must Know

May be seen in secretions such as sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage of patients with severe asthma.

Curschmann spiralsCharcot-Leyden crystals
  • Represent excessive mucus / mucus plugs formed from subepithelial mucus glands of bronchi
  • May also be seen in chronic bronchitis
Rhomboid-shaped crystals seen in bronchial asthma
Figure 31. Curschmann spirals (L) and Charcot-Leyden crystals (R) [Lecturer's PPT] · p. 14
Exam Trap (Concept Checkpoint) Narrowing of the lumen is a classic histologic feature of asthma, but it is not seen in sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage specimens. Only the mucus/mucus plugs (Curschmann spirals) and rhomboid crystals (Charcot-Leyden) appear in secretions.

Clinical Course

  • Immediate intervention would render resolution of wheezing and dyspnea
  • Acute severe asthma (status asthmaticus): paroxysmal cough persists for days and weeks, sometimes leading to airway obstruction, extreme hypoxia and cyanosis, and eventually death
Clinical Cue
  • Most distinct gross finding in fatal status asthmaticus → occluded bronchi & bronchioles by thick mucus plugs.
  • Episodic wheezing after minor respiratory infections, no family history, normal IgE → non-atopic asthma.

E. Bronchiectasis p. 15–16

Definition Must Know

A lung disorder characterized by the destruction of smooth muscle and elastic tissue in the bronchial wall due to necrotizing inflammation from persistent or severe infections, leading to permanent dilation of the bronchi and bronchioles.

Predisposing factors

  • Infections — persistent, severe necrotizing: S. aureus, Klebsiella, MTB, and fungal infections like Aspergillosis
  • Genetic / hereditary disorders — e.g., cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia
    • In cystic fibrosis, defective chloride transport in exocrine tissues → thick, sticky mucus accumulates → airway obstruction → lung infections → progressive airway damage
  • Bronchial obstruction — common causes are tumors, foreign bodies, and impaction of mucus

Pathogenesis

The 2 major factors that contribute to the pathogenesis Must Know

  1. Loss of the clearing system of the muco-ciliary apparatus
    • Can follow either obstruction (ex. foreign body), a defect in the dynein arms of the cilia (Kartagener syndrome), or abnormal mucus (cystic fibrosis)
  2. Presence of infection
    • Defect in the clearance system → accumulation of secretions, bacterial overgrowth, infection, and atelectasis → chronic infection damages the integrity of the bronchial wall → dilatation

Two factors must be present: Obstruction + Infection. Interplay of the 2 factors → prolonged inflammation → bronchial wall destruction and dilation.

Figure 32 and 33 — pathogenesis (recreated)

Obstruction + Chronic infection
  • Infection → accumulated secretions ← Obstruction (impairment of muco-ciliary mechanism)
↓
Inflammation → inflammatory damage to the bronchial wall
↓
Necrosis & permanent dilatation of airway
↓
Irreversible dilation of the airways (Bronchiectasis)
Persistent infection (lecturer emphasis)
  • Infection causes development and propagation of the lesion through the vicious cycle of inflammation and tissue damage → disturbance of the mucociliary apparatus → bacterial colonization, neutrophil activation → marked inflammation and destruction of tissue.
  • Post-lab clarification: The development and propagation of this lesion requires continued persistence of the initial insult or infection → TRUE.

Morphology

GrossHistology
  • Prominent dilation of the lumen of the airways
  • Usually affects the lower lobes bilaterally, most severe in the most distal bronchi and bronchioles
  • Intense, acute and chronic inflammation within the walls of the bronchi and bronchioles
  • Layers of the bronchial walls (smooth muscle and cartilage) are indiscernible and replaced by inflammatory cells/cytokines
Figure 35. Gross bronchiectasis — markedly dilated bronchi extending to the periphery · p. 16
Figure 36. Microscopic bronchiectasis — loss of mucosal lining and destruction of bronchial wall layers · p. 16
Figure 34. Bronchiectasis due to underlying cystic fibrosis — mucus plugs (arrows) dilating and obstructing the airway · p. 15

Clinical Features / Course

  • Presents with severe, persistent cough with expectoration of mucopurulent, sometimes foul-smelling (bloody) sputum
  • The vicious cycle may lead to advanced complications: lung abscess, empyema, cor pulmonale, and respiratory failure
  • Marked dyspnea & cyanosis develops as a result of obstructive ventilatory insufficiency
    • With better antibiotics and physiotherapy, outcomes have improved
  • Other less frequent complications: cor pulmonale, metastatic brain abscess & amyloidosis (especially if not promptly treated)
Exam Trap (Concept Checkpoint)
  • Bronchiectasis is permanent dilation, NOT narrowing, of bronchi and bronchioles.
  • Bronchial obstruction is a predisposing factor but is not a congenital or hereditary condition (cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, and Kartagener syndrome are).

VII. Chronic Diffuse Interstitial (Restrictive) Diseases p. 16–17

  • Characterized by reduced lung volumes either because of:
    • Alteration in the lung parenchyma
    • Disease of the pleura, chest wall, or neuromuscular apparatus
  • Reduced compliance = reduced gas exchange
  • Characterized predominantly by fibrosis and inflammation of lung interstitium associated with pulmonary function studies
  • Diffuse · Heterogeneous
  • Categories based on histology & clinical features: Fibrosing, Granulomatous, Eosinophilic smoking related, Others (Langerhans cell histiocytosis, pulmonary alveolar proteinosis)
  • Many of the disease entities are of unknown cause and pathogenesis

A. Common Features

Manifestations
Dyspnea, tachypnea, end-inspiratory crackles, clubbing of digits, and cyanosis (in advanced stages)
Pulmonary function tests
↓ vital capacity, ↓ total lung capacity, ↓ residual volume, and ↓ lung compliance
Sequelae
Secondary pulmonary hypertension and right-sided heart failure with cor pulmonale may result
Must Know
  • Restrictive pulmonary diseases are characterized predominantly by inflammation and fibrosis.
  • The manifestations DO NOT include sputum production.

B. Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF)

  • Also known as Cryptogenic fibrosing alveolitis
  • Histologic pattern of fibrosis — usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP)
    • UIP can also be seen in other diseases, hence IPF must be distinguished based on other clinical, laboratory, and histologic features
  • Etiology: unknown
  • A specific form of progressive, chronic, fibrosing interstitial pneumonia
  • Primarily occurring in older adults, limited to the lungs
  • IPF is a prototypic of restrictive lung diseases Must Know

Pathogenesis

Arises in a genetically predisposed individual who is prone to aberrant repair of recurrent alveolar epithelial cell injuries caused by environmental exposures.

Original hypothesis (left)New hypothesis (right)
  • Generalized inflammation progressed to widespread parenchymal fibrosis
  • Anti-inflammatory agents and immune modulators failed in modifying the natural course of the disease
  • An unknown endogenous or environmental stimulus disrupts the homeostasis of the alveolar epithelial cells
  • Results in a diffused aberrant epithelial cell repair that eventually leads to a fibrotic lung
Figure 37. Original vs new hypothesis on the pathogenesis of IPF [Lecturer's PPT] · p. 17

Morphology Must Know

GrossHistology
  • Cobblestone appearance of the outer (pleural) surface of the lung
  • Cut-section: firm, rubbery, with wide areas of fibrosis preferentially seen in the lower lobes
  • Hallmark: patchy interstitial fibrosis (may vary in intensity and age of lesion)
  • Dense fibrosis causes destruction of alveolar architecture, characterized as honeycomb fibrosis
  • Histologic pattern: usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP)
Figure 38. Morphology of IPF — cobblestone pleural surface (L), honeycomb fibrosis (R) · p. 17

Clinical Course

  • Variable and unpredictable
    • Usually slow, progressive respiratory failure
    • Some patients have acute exacerbations and a rapid downhill course
    • Median survival is 3.8 years after diagnosis
  • Gradual deterioration in pulmonary function despite medical treatment
  • Lung transplantation is the ONLY definitive treatment

C. Pneumoconiosis p. 17–18

Definition Must Know

  • A generic term referring to a group of lung diseases that are occupationally related, restrictive, and arise due to chronic inhalation of inorganic (mineral dust) and organic dust encountered in the workplace
  • Lecturer: group of chronic fibrosing diseases of the lung resulting from exposure to organic and inorganic particulates, most commonly mineral dust

Pathogenesis of Pneumoconiosis

Pulmonary alveolar macrophages play a central role in the pathogenesis of lung injury by promoting inflammation and producing fibrogenic cytokines. Must Know

Silica, coal, asbestos have similar pathways.

Phagocytosis of the inhaled inorganic particulates by macrophages
↓
Activates the inflammasome and stimulates inflammatory mediators
↓
Activation of fibroblasts
↓
Fibrosis + collagen deposition
Figure 39 / 45. Pathogenesis of pneumoconiosis — silica, coal, asbestos [Lecturer's PPT] · p. 18, 20
Macrophages → mitochondria damage, ROS production, DNA damage. Epithelial cells → apoptosis. Treg: TGF-β, PDGF. Teff: IL-1β, IL-4, IFN-γ. Others: TNF-α, gremlin → myofibroblast → collagen → fibrotic response.

Factors influencing pathogenesis

  • Dust retention: determined by dust concentration, duration of exposure, and effectiveness of the mucociliary apparatus
    • Any influence (ex. smoking) that impairs mucociliary clearance significantly increases accumulation of dust particles
  • Particle size: 1–5 μm (diameter) most dangerous particle size Must Know
    • This size can reach the deeper portions of the lungs such as the terminal alveoli
  • Particle solubility and cytotoxicity: influenced by particle size
    • Smaller particle = higher solubility Must Know → more likely to produce rapid acute lung injury
    • Larger particles resist dissolution → tend to evoke a fibrosing pneumoconiosis
  • Particle uptake by epithelial cells: interactions of fibroblasts with interstitial macrophages
  • Activation of the inflammasome: after phagocytosis of certain particles by macrophages. This innate immune response amplifies the intensity and duration of the local reaction
  • Tobacco smoking: worsens the effects of inhaled mineral dust, particularly asbestos

Coal Workers Pneumoconiosis (CWP)

Lung disorder caused by inhalation of coal particles. Can give rise to a spectrum of lesions:

LesionSeverityFeatures
1. AnthracosisBenignLittle to no pulmonary dysfunction
2. Coal macule / noduleBenignLittle to no pulmonary dysfunction
3. Complicated CWPSevere form
  • Also known as Progressive Massive Fibrosis (PMF)
  • Lung function is compromised
  • Described as severe blackened lung
  • Gross: 1–10 cm blackened scars
  • Microscopic: dense collagen + pigment + local areas of ischemic necrotic lung tissue
Figure 36 (CWP). Anthracosis, coal macule/nodule, complicated CWP · p. 18
Figure 40. Complicated CWP — severe blackened lung with large scars · p. 18

Clinical course of CWP

  • Usually benign and causes minimal pulmonary dysfunction
  • Only when there is PMF in complicated CWP does it compromise pulmonary function → pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale
  • No convincing evidence that CWP increases susceptibility to tuberculosis, unlike silicosis
  • CWP does not predispose to cancer in the absence of smoking
Must KnowCWP ≠ Cancer or tuberculosis

D. Silicosis p. 18–19

  • Most prevalent chronic occupational disease in the world
  • Caused by inhalation of crystalline silicon dioxide (silica)
    • Crystalline form: more fibrogenic (including quartz)
    • Amorphous form

Pathogenesis

Exposure to free silica → inhaled silica is phagocytosed by macrophages
↓
Interaction of crystalline silica and hydrogen ions in cell membranes → damage to lysosome membrane (peroxidation of lipid membrane) → generation of oxygen-free radicals → further intracellular damage
↓
Release of proteolytic enzymes to cytoplasm → cause death of macrophage
↓
Further release of enzymes into the lungs. Continued silica exposure and frequent macrophage damage → alteration in macrophage function → activation of humoral and cellular immunity
↓
Release of inflammatory cytokines IL-1 and IL-8, free radicals, and growth factors → cytokines activate collagen synthesis
↓
Fibrotic reaction initiated

Morphology of Silicosis

GrossHistologic
  • Upper lobe is contracted into a small dark mass of lung tissue
  • Egg shell calcification in the enlarged hilar lymph node Must Know
Silicotic nodule that has coalesced, composed of dense collagenous tissue
Figure 42. Gross (L) and histologic (R) morphology of silicosis — contracted upper lobe (yellow arrow), coalesced silicotic nodule · p. 19

Clinical Course of Silicosis

  • Often slow & insidious
  • Inhalation of crystalline silica over prolonged periods (10–30 years) promotes classic fibrotic nodules
    • Nodules most often seen on the upper zones of the lungs and subpleural areas on chest x-ray
  • Early course: pulmonary function may be normal or moderately affected
  • May continue to worsen once PMF sets in with dyspnea. Course may continue even if no longer exposed
  • Depressed cell mediated immunity → increased susceptibility to tuberculosis, since silicosis inhibits the ability of pulmonary macrophages to kill phagocytosed mycobacteria
  • Also an increased risk of developing lung cancer

E. Asbestos-Related Disease p. 19–20

Asbestosis

  • Diffuse interstitial pulmonary fibrosis consequent to inhalation of excess asbestos fibers
  • Associated with heavy, cumulative asbestos dose
  • Latent period from initial exposure to disease manifestation is 20 years or more

Asbestos can give rise to a variety of disorders

  • Simple to localized fibrous plaques, rarely diffuse pleural fibrosis
  • Pleural effusion, recurrent
  • Asbestosis
  • Lung carcinomas
  • Malignant mesothelioma
  • Laryngeal and other extrapulmonary neoplasms, including colon CA

Pathogenesis — depends on the form of asbestos fiber

Amphibole formSerpentine Chrysotile form
  • More pathogenic due to aerodynamic configuration (straight and stiff)
  • "Bad form" → causes malignant mesothelioma
  • Configuration allows them to lodge in deeper portions of the lung when inhaled
  • More flexible, curled structures
  • More likely to be impacted in the upper airways and removed by the mucociliary apparatus
  • Asbestos can act as both a tumor initiator or promoter
    • Oncogenic effects mediated by free radicals generated by asbestos fibers, which preferentially localize in the distal portion of the lungs
  • Shares the same pathogenesis with silicosis
Figure 43. Asbestos types — amphibole (straight, stiff) vs serpentine (curled) · p. 19

Morphology of Asbestosis — Asbestos bodies Must Know

  • Presence of asbestos bodies in the lung tissue is diagnostic
  • Distinguishing characteristic from other disorders that form diffuse interstitial fibrosis
  • Appear as golden-brown fusiform or beaded rods with a translucent center, consisting of asbestos fibers coated with iron-containing proteinaceous material
Figure 44. Asbestos body — golden-brown beaded rod with translucent center · p. 20

Clinical Course of Asbestosis

  • Similar to other diffuse interstitial lung diseases
  • Clinical manifestations: dyspnea & abnormal lung function
    • Rarely appear fewer than 10 years of exposure
    • More common after 20–30 years of exposure
  • Can remain static or progress to respiratory failure, cor pulmonale, and death
  • Can be complicated by lung or pleural cancer and has a grimmer outcome
PneumoconiosisDustKey morphologyLocationAssociations / clues
CWPCoal particlesAnthracosis → coal macule → PMF (1–10 cm blackened scars)Upper lobes (PMF)≠ cancer or TB
SilicosisCrystalline silica (quartz)Silicotic nodules of dense collagen, egg shell calcification of hilar nodesUpper zones, subpleural↑ TB susceptibility, ↑ lung cancer, most prevalent occupational disease
AsbestosisAsbestos fibers (amphibole worst)Asbestos bodies (diagnostic), diffuse interstitial fibrosis, pleural plaquesDistal/lower lungsMesothelioma, lung CA, latency ≥ 20 yrs

F. Complication of Therapies p. 20

Pulmonary complications in the form of interstitial fibrosis may result as a side effect of either chemotherapy (drug-induced) or radiation therapy (radiation-induced).

Drug-induced

  • Cytotoxic drugs used for cancer therapy damage the lungs and cause fibrosis as a result of direct toxicity and by stimulating the influx of inflammatory cells (into the alveoli)
DrugClinical use and effect
Bleomycin & MethotrexateCytotoxic drugs used in cancer therapy that cause pneumonitis and interstitial fibrosis
AmiodaroneAnti-arrhythmic drug which causes significant pneumonitis (5–15%)
NitrofurantoinUTI
AspirinAnalgesic, antipyretic, anti-inflammatory
Beta antagonistCVD such as hypertension
ACE inhibitorsCough (common)

Radiation-induced

  • Radiation pneumonitis: known complication of therapeutic radiation of thoracic tumors such as those in the lungs, breast, esophagus, and mediastinum

G. Granulomatous Diseases — Sarcoidosis p. 20–21

  • Inflammatory disease that affects multiple organs in the body
    • Common in lungs and hilar lymph nodes
  • Typical clinical picture: young adult below 40, higher prevalence in women. Highest in US (particularly among Blacks), rare among Southeast Asians and Chinese
  • Etiology is unknown, but caused by immunologic, genetic, and environmental factors
    • Disorder of immune regulation in a genetically predisposed individual

Table 10. Factors affecting the pathogenesis

FactorEvidence
Immunologic
  • Intra-alveolar and interstitial accumulation of CD4+ T cells, resulting in CD4/CD8 ratios ranging from 5:1 → pathogenic involvement of CD4+ helper T cells
  • Increased T cell derived Th1 cytokines (IL-2 and IFN-γ)
  • Impaired dendritic cell function
GeneticFamilial and racial clustering of cases, association with certain HLA genotypes
EnvironmentalNot elaborated, no present information in book

Morphology of Sarcoidosis

GrossHistology
  • Lung and hilar lymph nodes are common sites
  • In advanced cases: visible, enlarged, non-caseating, coalesced nodes in the hilar and mediastinal region
  • Presence of multiple, small, non-caseating granulomas
  • Scattered within lung interstitium
Figure 46. Gross & histologic morphology of sarcoidosis — enlarged hilar nodes and non-caseating granulomas · p. 21

Schaumann bodies and Asteroid bodies Must Know

  • Distinguishes sarcoidosis from other granulomatous lesions in the lungs
  • Seen in 60% of granulomas
  • Schaumann bodies: laminated concretions found within giant cells
  • Asteroid bodies: stellate inclusions, also found within giant cells
Figure 47. Schaumann bodies (L) and asteroid bodies (R) · p. 21

Clinical Course of Sarcoidosis

  • Protean manifestations, unpredictable course/prognosis
  • Since sarcoidosis is systemic, it may present with diverse clinical features
OutcomeProportion
Recover with minimal or no residual manifestationsMajority (65–70%)
Permanent loss of some lung function or permanent visual impairmentMinority (20%)
Succumb to progressive pulmonary fibrosis and cor pulmonale (some die of cardiac or CNS damage)Worst (10–15%)
Exam TrapSarcoidosis is a systemic NON-caseating granulomatous disorder — "caseating" is the trap.

H. Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis p. 21

  • Aka Allergic alveolitis
  • Results from inhalation of organic dust containing antigens made up of spores, fungi, animal protein, or bacterial products
  • Leads to exaggerated immune response — both Type 3 and 4 hypersensitivity can occur depending on case

Table 11. Examples

DiseaseExposure
Farmer's lungDust generated from humid harvested hay that permits proliferation of spores from thermophilic bacteria
Pigeon breeder's lung (bird fancier's disease)Provoked by proteins from serum, excreta, or feathers of birds

Clinical Course

  • Manifestations vary: recurring episodes of fever, cough, dyspnea, and leukocytosis
    • Acute attacks may occur following inhalation of antigenic dust in sensitized patients
  • Majority respond well to corticosteroid therapy
  • If exposure continues, a chronic form supervenes → progressive fibrosis, dyspnea, and cyanosis

Morphology — Histologic changes

PhaseFindings
Acute phase
  • Interstitial pneumonitis
  • Noncaseating granuloma
Advanced, chronic phaseInterstitial fibrosis with honeycombing & obliterative bronchiolitis

Core Definitions

  • Type I pneumocytes: 90% of surface, gas exchange, easily injured. Type II: 10%, surfactant, repair, more resistant to injury.
  • Dyspnea: distinguish pulmonary (inability to get a deep breath, ↑ work of breathing) vs cardiac (suffocation, air hunger, chest heaviness).
  • Pulmonary hypoplasia: incomplete development of one or both lungs. Premature babies born before 28 weeks AOG. Early respiratory distress, cyanosis, tachypnea, hypoxia, hypercapnia, acidosis.
  • Foregut cysts: abnormal budding/detachment of primitive foregut. 3 types: bronchogenic (most common, pseudostratified columnar ciliated), esophageal (squamous), enteric.
  • Pulmonary sequestration: lung tissue without normal connection to airway, supplied by aorta. Extralobar = infants, mass. Intralobar = older children, recurrent infection.
  • Atelectasis: loss of lung volume due to incomplete expansion.
  • Pulmonary edema: extravasation of fluid from pulmonary vasculature into interstitium and alveoli.
  • ALI: abrupt hypoxemia + bilateral infiltrates, no cardiac failure. ARDS: clinical term for severe ALI. Histology = DAD.
  • Emphysema: irreversible abnormal enlargement of airspaces distal to terminal bronchioles with destruction of walls and little or no fibrosis.
  • Chronic bronchitis: persistent cough with sputum ≥ 3 months/year in ≥ 2 consecutive years, no other identifiable cause.
  • COPD: emphysema + chronic bronchitis grouped clinically, irreversible airflow obstruction (with bronchiectasis).
  • Asthma: chronic airway inflammation + variable expiratory obstruction, largely reversible.
  • Bronchiectasis: destruction of smooth muscle and elastic tissue of bronchial wall from necrotizing inflammation → permanent dilation of bronchi and bronchioles.
  • Restrictive diseases: reduced lung volumes, predominantly inflammation and fibrosis, no sputum production.
  • IPF (cryptogenic fibrosing alveolitis): prototype restrictive disease, unknown etiology, UIP pattern.
  • Pneumoconiosis: chronic fibrosing lung diseases from inhaled organic/inorganic particulates, most commonly mineral dust.
  • Sarcoidosis: systemic inflammatory disease, non-caseating granulomas, lungs and hilar nodes.
  • Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (allergic alveolitis): organic dust antigens, Type 3 and 4 hypersensitivity.

Mechanisms & Essential Sequences

ARDS pathogenesis (4 phases)

  1. Endothelial activation: alveolar macrophages detect injury → IL-1, TNF → activate/damage endothelium
  2. Neutrophil adhesion/extravasation: proteases, ROS, cytokines → damage Type I pneumocytes → vicious cycle
  3. Intra-alveolar fluid + hyaline membrane: ↑ permeability, Type I necrosis, Type II injured → ↓ surfactant, protein-rich fluid + debris → pink waxy hyaline membranes → impaired ventilation and perfusion
  4. Resolution: slow. Macrophages clear debris → TGF-β, PDGF → fibrosis. Type II pneumocytes proliferate to replace Type I

Two initiating events: damage to endothelium + Type I pneumocytes, and inflammation. 30 min after insult: ↑ IL-8.

Emphysema — 2 critical imbalances

  • Protease-antiprotease: α1-antitrypsin deficiency → panacinar. Smoking → neutrophil influx → elastase → digestion of elastic tissue
  • Oxidant-antioxidant: heavy smoking → centriacinar. Tobacco ROS deplete antioxidants and inactivate antiproteases → functional α1-AT deficiency

Chronic bronchitis

Inhaled irritant (tobacco) → airway inflammation → hypertrophy of submucosal glands → mucus hypersecretion → acute bronchitis episodes / productive cough. Goblet cell excess → submucosal gland hyperplasia/hypertrophy → bronchiolitis → fibrosis.

Atopic asthma

Allergen → Th2 → cytokines → B cells make IgE + eosinophil recruitment → IgE on mast cells → re-exposure cross-links IgE on Fc receptors → early phase (bronchospasm, ↑ permeability, mucus, leukocyte recruitment) → late phase (leukocyte mediators).

Bronchiectasis

Obstruction + infection → loss of mucociliary clearance (foreign body, Kartagener dynein defect, cystic fibrosis abnormal mucus) → secretions accumulate → bacterial overgrowth → chronic infection → wall destruction → irreversible dilation. Persistence of infection is required for propagation.

Pneumoconiosis

Macrophage phagocytosis of particulate → inflammasome activation → inflammatory mediators → fibroblast activation → fibrosis + collagen. Silica, coal, asbestos share this pathway. Silica also damages lysosomes → free radicals → macrophage death → IL-1, IL-8 → collagen synthesis.

Common Confusions & Exam Traps

  • ARDS vs ALI: ARDS = clinical, ALI = pathologic. Both show DAD.
  • Centriacinar spares distal alveoli and is upper lobe. Panacinar is uniform and lower zone.
  • Emphysema has destruction without fibrosis. Restrictive disease is fibrosis.
  • Asthma is reversible. COPD and bronchiectasis are irreversible.
  • Narrowing of lumen is histologic, not seen in sputum/BAL. Sputum shows Curschmann spirals and Charcot-Leyden crystals.
  • Curschmann spirals may also be seen in chronic bronchitis.
  • Bronchiectasis = dilation, not narrowing. Bronchial obstruction is not a hereditary cause (CF, PCD, Kartagener are).
  • Sarcoidosis = NON-caseating granulomas.
  • CWP does not increase TB or cancer. Silicosis does increase TB and lung cancer.
  • Egg shell calcification = silicosis, not asbestosis. Ferruginous/asbestos bodies = asbestosis.
  • In restrictive disease FEV1 is reduced but the ratio is normal.
  • Restrictive manifestations do not include sputum production.
  • Contraction atelectasis is the only irreversible type.
  • Digital clubbing is non-specific, also in chronic hypoxemic heart disease.

Warnings & Complications

  • COPD deaths: right-sided heart failure, pneumothorax (emphysema), bacterial infection (bronchitis), acute respiratory failure.
  • Cor pulmonale + secondary pulmonary hypertension → poor prognosis (emphysema, chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis, PMF, IPF, sarcoidosis).
  • Chronic bronchitis epithelium → metaplasia/dysplasia → cancer.
  • Status asthmaticus → extreme hypoxia, cyanosis, death. Gross: mucus-plugged airways.
  • Bronchiectasis → lung abscess, empyema, cor pulmonale, respiratory failure, metastatic brain abscess, amyloidosis.
  • Asbestos → lung CA, mesothelioma (amphibole), laryngeal and colon CA. Smoking worsens asbestos effects.
  • Drug-induced fibrosis: bleomycin, methotrexate. Amiodarone pneumonitis. ACE inhibitors cough.
  • Radiation pneumonitis after thoracic radiation (lung, breast, esophagus, mediastinum).
